transcript:
Meeting: Threaded kernel scheduling deep dive - lockstep CUDA Graphs vs dynamic replay
Date: 2029-05-06 16:00 UTC
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Greta Alvarez (Redwood SE), Oscar Reed (Redwood SRE); Samir Rao (Vantage Lead ML Infra), Evelyn Walker (Vantage SRE), Dr. Noah Kim (Vantage ML Eng), Priya Desai (Vantage Security)

Summary: quick triage of instability and latency tail in customer on-prem tests; focus on kernel scheduling strategies (CUDA Graph lockstep capture/replay vs dynamic per-request replay), interactions with KV cache persistence and batching heuristics, and quantization implications for TRT-LLM vs vLLM execution paths. Agreement to run targeted microbenchmarks on customer's cluster with NVLink and share results.

Topics: kernel scheduling, cuda graph capture, dynamic replay, kv cache eviction, batching hysteresis, quantization edge-cases, vpc/on-prem constraints, profiling artifacts (nvprof, nsight, nvtx)

Action items (also in metadata): see list

00:00 Maya Chen: ok hey everyone thanks for joining uh we're gonna jump right in, this is a follow up to the failed run you sent last week where the tail latency spikes after about 30 minutes, right?
00:07 Samir Rao: yeah, thanks Maya. we saw two things: intermittent 99.9 spikes and occasional cudaGraph launch failures that required a service restart. it's noisy but repeatable after warmup.
00:15 Liam Patel: quick clarification — when you say launch failures, is that graph capture error during model init or runtime kernel mismatch?
00:20 Evelyn Walker: it's during runtime, after we hit a certain sequence length pattern. there was an error that looked like a kernel exec mismatch. log's attached in the sheet but it's messy.
00:29 Greta Alvarez: okay so we've seen that pattern when kernels switch path mid-episode — like persistent KV cache plus dynamic attention lengths cause the runtime to choose a different kernel set and cudagraph replay doesn't match the new path.
00:40 Dr. Noah Kim: hmm interesting. our workload is multi-tenant, a mix of short chat-ish prompts and long document syntheses. we assumed cudagraphs would give consistent latency but seems brittle.
00:51 Liam Patel: yes, cudagraph lockstep is great for stable control flow — you capture an exact kernel sequence and replay with very low overhead — but if the runtime has heuristics that switch kernel implementations (e.g., different tiling for long vs short sequences, quant path selection) you'll get mismatch. sometimes the API throws a launch-time assertion, other times subtle memory corruption.
01:08 Maya Chen: can you describe the model/config that's failing — quantized? batch sizes? kv cache persistence?
01:13 Samir Rao: model is a 22B finetuned LLaMA derivative, we've applied mixed int8 quant with per-channel scaling on weights. batch sizes are variable: 1-4 in hosted mode, bursts to 8 in batch windows. KV cache is persisted across requests for same session.
01:28 Greta Alvarez: mixed-int8 + cudagraphs is a known brittle combo. quantization changes kernel selection; TRT-LLM tends to select int8 fused kernels, vLLM style dynamic exec tends to fall back to fp16 kernels if scales mismatch. that path diff can break a captured graph.
01:43 Samir Rao: ok so is the recommendation then to disable cudagraphs for quantized models?
01:47 Liam Patel: not necessarily. there are patterns. Option A: capture multiple graphs keyed by execution path (sequence length bucket, quantization variant) and route at runtime — that's what we call a "multi-graph" strategy. Option B: use dynamic replay (no cudagraph) which is more flexible but higher per-token cost. Option C: hybrid — try cudagraph for the dominant steady-state path and fallback to dynamic when a path mismatch is detected.
02:09 Evelyn Walker: multi-graph sounds heavy; we'd need to store graphs and have quick tiebreakers to pick the right one. we're on-prem with limited disk and NVLink cluster.
02:18 Oscar Reed: storage for graphs is cheap; the complexity is correctness: you have to ensure kernel versions, cuda driver, and model codegen are stable. we've seen graph replay mismatch when a small kernel patch landed in the driver.
02:29 Dr. Noah Kim: you'd also need to consider KV cache layout — does multi-graph strategy assume same KV offset/layout?
02:34 Greta Alvarez: yes, that's the sticky part. If KV cache layout changes (like switching from interleaved to contiguous banks due to a different kernel path) the captured graph's pointer arithmetic can be invalid. we saw that in profiling: nvtx markers showed the KV load kernel changed tensor ordering.
02:49 Liam Patel: practical approach: 1) instrument and capture nvprof/nsight traces across failure window, 2) run a sequence-bucketing benchmark to identify dominant paths, 3) generate graphs per bucket and validate with fuzzed prompts, 4) implement cheap runtime checks to detect path mismatches and fall back.
03:10 Maya Chen: can we go over the microbench we suggest? include metrics we expect to compare lockstep vs dynamic.
03:15 Liam Patel: sure. script does: cold start capture; warmup 5k tokens; run 500 prompts per bucket (buckets: <=64 tokens, 65-512, 512-2048); measure p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, cudaGraph failure rate, and KV cache hit ratio. also capture per-kernel times, and nvtx annotated timeline.
03:36 Samir Rao: what delta is realistic between lockstep and dynamic? we saw sometimes 20-40% lower p50 with graph replay.
03:42 Greta Alvarez: yes when graph matches steady-state you'll see 25-45% lower per-token latency and 10-30% higher throughput due to reduced dispatch overhead. but mismatch cost is high — a single fallback or crash kills throughput and requires restart in your setup.
03:57 Priya Desai: from a security angle — if you need to store multiple graphs or logs, we need to ensure those artifacts are encrypted and don't contain model secrets. also SOC2 concerns for on-prem pipelines.
04:09 Maya Chen: noted — we'll include a trimmed security checklist. Greta, Liam will include storage/encryption recommendations.
04:15 Liam Patel: one nuance — TRT-LLM int8 kernels are highly optimized and can have different warp-to-memory patterns; we measured an int8 fused attention kernel that reduces global memory by ~30% but uses a banked shared memory layout. that layout change is what triggered mismatches.
04:33 Dr. Noah Kim: are there heuristics to detect when the kernel mapper will flip to the fused int8 kernel before capture?
04:38 Greta Alvarez: yes some runtime heuristics are predictable: sequence length, batch_size, quant_flag, and model block size. you can approximate a decision-tree for kernel selection. but there are edge cases where occupancy and free memory nudges the runtime to choose a different kernel — e.g., when NVLink placement moves tensors across GPUs.
04:55 Evelyn Walker: NVLink — we should mention our cluster is a 4xA100 NVLink fabric, multi-tenant, with PCIe spillover when some jobs allocate big tensor buffers.
05:05 Liam Patel: that can impact kernel selection at runtime: if a big job causes fragmentation, an otherwise fused kernel might fall back to a non-fused path because it couldn't allocate the scratch buffer. That explains intermittent behavior after ~30min when other tenants start jobs.
05:20 Samir Rao: so isolation — Dedicated or Private VPC — would mitigate that?
05:24 Maya Chen: Right, Redwood Dedicated with reserved capacity or Private on-prem with pinned GPUs reduces noisy neighbor; you'll still have kernel selection variability from sequence/batching, but not from cross-tenant fragmentation.
05:35 Priya Desai: for Private deployment we need KMS integration and audit logs; please include guidance on storing graphs in a customer-managed KMS-encrypted bucket.
05:43 Greta Alvarez: will do. back to quant: another problem is dynamic quant scales. Per-tensor vs per-channel scales can cause numerical range differences that lead to different kernel variants (one supports per-channel ephemeral scales). That changes instruction mix.
05:58 Liam Patel: benchmarking note: compare three execution modes: (1) TRT-LLM cudagraph capture, (2) vLLM dynamic with continuous batching and async KV prefetch, (3) hybrid with guarded capture and software fallback. measure latency tail and failure rate.
06:17 Dr. Noah Kim: what about KV cache prefetch granularity? we observe prefetching too aggressively causes memory pressure and then evictions, which seems to correlate with spikes.
06:26 Greta Alvarez: yes, prefetching heuristics matter. aggressive prefetching is good for throughput but increases memory churn and can push the runtime into a different kernel path (because it changes available scratch space). tune prefetch depth and prefer on-demand prefetch for heterogeneous workloads.
06:40 Liam Patel: we also suggest a small modification to the batching heuristics: use a latency SLO-aware bucketed batching — keep a small fast lane for single-token interactive requests (no graph) and a heavy lane for batched offline requests (capture graphs).
06:53 Samir Rao: that fits our product — interactive triage vs bulk generation. can Redwood help implement the two-lane routing logic?
06:58 Maya Chen: yes we can provide a routing policy and sample middleware. Liam, Greta will provide a config template.
07:04 Evelyn Walker: quick question on tools — what traces do you want? nsight timeline, nvprof per-kernel, driver logs, and Redwood's runtime debug trace?
07:12 Liam Patel: collect all those. nvprof/nvtx for kernel timing, nsight for occupancy and warps, dmesg/driver logs for any kernel driver mismatches, and Redwood runtime debug which includes kernel selection decision points. we'll provide a small wrapper to correlate timestamps.
07:27 Dr. Noah Kim: any recommended quick checks we can run to reproduce the failure before giving you access?
07:31 Greta Alvarez: yes: 1) run a synthetic workload that alternates short/long sequences every 5 minutes, 2) add background allocations to simulate tenant noise, 3) run with quant enabled and then with quant disabled to see delta. these three will likely trigger the path flip quickly.
07:47 Priya Desai: compliance question again — can the debug wrapper redact prompt content? we can't share PHI.
07:52 Maya Chen: absolutely, we'll provide a redaction mode that hashes prompt text and only shares token lengths and timing.
07:57 Samir Rao: perfect. about fallback recovery — currently our service restarts on graph launch failure. can Redwood runtime do graceful fallback without restarting?
08:03 Liam Patel: yes, runtime can catch a graph replay mismatch and switch to dynamic kernel path for that request or session. it increases latency but keeps service alive. restarting is a brute force mitigation we want to avoid.
08:15 Evelyn Walker: is there any chance fallback will corrupt model state?
08:19 Greta Alvarez: not if implemented carefully. ensure that graph capture doesn't mutate model buffers in unexpected ways and that you reset any temp alloc counters. we have checksums we run post-capture to validate buffer integrity.
08:30 Dr. Noah Kim: curious about numbers — if we go hybrid, what's the expected p99 reduction vs pure dynamic?
08:35 Liam Patel: based on our internal tests on similar 20–30B models, hybrid can give you ~20% lower p50 and reduce p99 by 15–30% compared to pure dynamic, while reducing failure rate versus capture-only by 70–90% depending on workload churn. very workload dependent.
08:52 Samir Rao: that seems promising. timeline: we can provision the cluster credentials by next week. when can you run the benchmark?
08:58 Maya Chen: SE team can run the first batch in ~5 business days after we get SSH and a sanitized prompt set. we'll share the benchmark script and the spreadsheet results.
09:07 Priya Desai: security deliverables — trimmed SOC2 doc, KMS integration steps, retention policy for traces.
09:14 Oscar Reed: we'll attach the checklist and sample IAM policy; also include instructions to encrypt graphs at rest.
09:20 Maya Chen: before we wrap, any final open questions?
09:23 Dr. Noah Kim: one small thing — we've seen a specific gpusmi / driver warning that coincides with failure events, could that be the root?
09:28 Liam Patel: driver mismatch is often root cause for cudagraph instability. please include exact driver/kernel versions in the artifacts — if there's a small mismatch between driver ABI and compiled kernels it causes undefined behavior.
09:39 Samir Rao: ok we'll capture that.
09:41 Maya Chen: recap — Redwood to run multi-bucket microbench, provide config template for two-lane routing, security checklist, and fallback middleware sample. Customer to provide sanitized prompt set, model weights (or at least a compatible stub), SSH access window, and driver logs. We'll aim to reconvene after initial benchmarks.
09:56 Evelyn Walker: thanks everyone.
09:58 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with the sheet and next steps.
10:01 [call ends]
